value.overview: The Black-banded Woodcreeper is a medium-sized, forest-dwelling songbird of the ovenbird family. It climbs trunks and large branches in search of insects and other small prey, using its strong bill to probe bark, vines, leaf clusters, and epiphytes. The species has a broad but patchy distribution from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon and local resident of mature, humid mountain forests.
value.classification: The Black-banded Woodcreeper belongs to the family Furnariidae and subfamily Dendrocolaptinae, the woodcreepers. Its scientific name is Dendrocolaptes picumnus; the Costa Rican population is generally assigned to the subspecies Dendrocolaptes picumnus costaricensis.
value.identification: This woodcreeper is about 24–30 cm long, with a long, stiff tail and a thick, straight, dark bill. The upperparts are brown with fine streaking, while the head and upper breast are more strongly marked. The lower breast and belly show distinctive dark horizontal barring, giving the species its common name. It can be separated from similar Costa Rican woodcreepers by its relatively large size, heavy bill, barred underparts, and preference for higher-elevation mature forest.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs discontinuously from southern Mexico through Central America and widely across northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce, local resident on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, mainly in the premontane and lower montane zones, roughly from 900 to 2,000 meters. It favors mature moist or wet forest with tall trees, including relatively undisturbed foothill and mountain forest. Records are local because suitable habitat is limited and the bird is difficult to detect.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and not considered a regular long-distance migrant. It generally remains in forested mountain areas throughout the year, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, especially for Costa Rica. Like other woodcreepers, it is believed to nest in natural tree cavities, often using existing holes rather than excavating them. The nest is made from small pieces of wood, bark, or other plant material, and the clutch is usually small. Breeding activity in Central America is reported mainly during the rainy-season months, but the timing and nesting details may vary among regions and remain incompletely documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-banded Woodcreeper feeds mainly on arthropods, including beetles, ants, cockroaches, spiders, and other invertebrates. It climbs trunks and branches in a spiral or hitching motion, probing bark crevices, vine tangles, dead leaves, bromeliads, and epiphytes with its bill. It may also take small vertebrates and flying insects. Individuals often forage alone or in pairs and may join mixed-species feeding flocks or follow army-ant swarms.
value.behavior: This species is usually encountered singly or in pairs in the middle and lower levels of mature forest. It moves methodically up trunks and along large branches, using its stiff tail for support. Its calls and song are whistled and can carry through dense forest, but the bird often remains concealed behind foliage and trunks. It may participate in mixed-species flocks, especially while searching for prey in structurally complex forest habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently classified as threatened.
